[[File:BBM equation - overtaking solitary waves animation.gif|thumb|416px|right|An animation of the overtaking of two [[solitary wave (water waves)|solitary waves]] according to the Benjamin–Bona–Mahony (BBM) equation. The [[wave height]]s of the solitary waves are 1.2 and 0.6, respectively, and their [[phase speed|celerities]] are 1.4 and 1.2. {{paragraph}}The upper graph is for a [[frame of reference]] moving with the average celerity of the solitary waves. The [[envelope (waves)|envelope]] of the overtaking waves is shown in grey: note that the maximum wave height reduces during the interaction. {{paragraph}}The lower graph (with a different vertical scale and in a stationary frame of reference) shows the [[oscillation|oscillatory]] tail produced by the interaction.<ref name="Bona_Pritchard_Scott">{{harvtxt|Bona|Pritchard|Scott|1980}}</ref> Thus, the solitary wave solutions of the BBM equation are not [[soliton]]s.]]
The '''Benjamin–Bona–Mahony equation''' ('''BBM equation''', also '''regularized long-wave equation'''; '''RLWE''') is the [[partial differential equation]]

:<math>u_t+u_x+uu_x-u_{xxt}=0.\,</math>

This equation was studied in {{harvs | author1-link=Brooke Benjamin | last=Benjamin | author2-link=Jerry L. Bona | last2= Bona | author3-link=John Joseph Mahony | last3= Mahony | year=1972 | txt=yes }} as an improvement of the [[Korteweg–de Vries equation]] (KdV equation) for  modeling  long [[surface gravity wave]]s of small amplitude – [[wave propagation|propagating]] uni-directionally in 1+1 dimensions. They show the stability and uniqueness of solutions to the BBM equation. This contrasts with the KdV equation, which is unstable in its high [[wavenumber]] components. Further, while the KdV equation has an infinite number of [[integral of motion|integrals of motion]], the BBM equation only has three.<ref name=BBM1972>{{harvs | author1-link=Brooke Benjamin | last=Benjamin | author2-link=Jerry L. Bona | last2= Bona | author3-link=John Joseph Mahony | last3= Mahony | year=1972 | txt=yes }}</ref><ref name=Olver>{{harvtxt|Olver|1979}}</ref>

Before, in 1966, this equation was introduced by [[Howell Peregrine|Peregrine]], in the study of [[undular bore]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Peregrine|1966}}</ref>

A generalized ''n''-dimensional version is given by<ref>{{harvtxt|Goldstein|Wichnoski|1980}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Avrin|Goldstein|1985}}</ref>

:<math>u_t-\nabla^2u_t+\operatorname{div}\,\varphi(u)=0.\,</math>

where <math>\varphi</math> is a sufficiently smooth function from <math>\mathbb R</math> to <math>\mathbb R^n</math>. {{harvtxt|Avrin|Goldstein|1985}} proved global existence of a solution in all dimensions.

==Solitary wave solution==
{{also|Cnoidal wave}}
The BBM equation possesses [[solitary wave (water waves)|solitary wave]] solutions of the form:<ref name=Olver/>

:<math>u = 3 \frac{c^2}{1-c^2} \operatorname{sech}^2 \frac12 \left( cx - \frac{ct}{1-c^2} + \delta \right),</math>

where sech is the [[hyperbolic secant]] function and <math>\delta</math> is a phase shift (by an initial horizontal displacement). For <math>|c|<1</math>, the solitary waves have a positive [[crest (physics)|crest]] elevation and travel in the positive <math>x</math>-direction with velocity <math>1/(1-c^2).</math> These solitary waves are not [[soliton]]s, i.e. after interaction with other solitary waves, an oscillatory tail is generated and the solitary waves have changed.<ref name="Bona_Pritchard_Scott"/><ref name=Olver/>

==Hamiltonian structure==
The BBM equation has a [[Hamiltonian system|Hamiltonian structure]], as it can be written as:<ref>{{harvtxt|Olver|1980}}</ref>

:<math>u_t = - \mathcal{D} \frac{\delta H}{\delta u},\,</math> with Hamiltonian <math>H = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \left( \tfrac12 u^2 + \tfrac16 u^3 \right)\, \text{d}x\,</math> and operator <math>\mathcal{D} = \left( 1 - \partial_x^2 \right)^{-1}\, \partial_x.</math> 

Here <math>\delta H/\delta u</math> is the [[calculus of variations|variation]] of the Hamiltonian <math>H(u)</math> with respect to <math>u(x),</math> and <math>\partial_x</math> denotes the partial differential operator with respect to <math>x.</math>

==Conservation laws==
The BBM equation possesses exactly three independent and non-trivial [[Conservation law (physics)|conservation law]]s.<ref name=Olver/> First <math>u</math> is replaced by <math>u=-v-1</math> in the BBM equation, leading to the equivalent equation:

:<math>v_t - v_{xxt} = v\, v_x.</math>

The three conservation laws then are:<ref name=Olver/>

:<math>
  \begin{align}
     v_t - \left( v_{xt} + \tfrac12 v^2 \right)_x & = 0, \\
     \left( \tfrac12 v^2 + \tfrac12 v_x^2 \right)_t - \left( v\, v_{xt} + \tfrac13 v^3 \right)_x & = 0,  \\
     \left( \tfrac13 v^3 \right)_t + \left( v_t^2 - v_{xt}^2 - v^2\, v_{xt} - \tfrac14 v^4 \right)_x & = 0.
  \end{align}
</math>

Which can easily expressed in terms of <math>u</math> by using <math>v=-u-1.</math>

==Linear dispersion==
The linearized version of the BBM equation is:

:<math>u_t + u_x - u_{xxt}=0.</math>

Periodic progressive wave solutions are of the form:

:<math>u = a\, \mathrm{e}^{i (k x-\omega t)},</math>

with <math>k</math> the [[wavenumber]] and <math>\omega</math> the [[angular frequency]]. The [[dispersion relation]] of the linearized BBM equation is<ref name=BBM1972/>

:<math>\omega_\mathrm{BBM} = \frac{k}{1+k^2}.</math>

Similarly, for the linearized KdV equation <math>u_t + u_x + u_{xxx} = 0</math> the dispersion relation is:<ref name=BBM1972/>

:<math>\omega_\mathrm{KdV} = k - k^3.</math>

This becomes unbounded and negative for <math>k\to\infty,</math> and the same applies to the [[phase velocity]] <math>\omega_\mathrm{KdV}/k</math> and [[group velocity]] <math>\mathrm{d}\omega_\mathrm{KdV}/\mathrm{d}k.</math> Consequently, the KdV equation gives waves travelling in the negative <math>x</math>-direction for high wavenumbers (short [[wavelengths]]). This is in contrast with its purpose as an approximation for uni-directional waves propagating in the positive <math>x</math>-direction.<ref name=BBM1972/>

The strong growth of frequency <math>\omega_\mathrm{KdV}</math> and phase speed with wavenumber <math>k</math> posed problems in the numerical solution of the KdV equation, while the BBM equation does not have these shortcomings.<ref name=BBM1972/>
